001JavaScript/FoundationPredict the event-loop output
The interview scenario

A click handler mixes synchronous logs, a resolved promise, queueMicrotask, and a zero-delay timer. What prints first?

How to answer

The output is A, E, C, D, B. Synchronous work runs to completion. The promise reaction and explicit microtask are queued in that order and run at the microtask checkpoint before the timer task. A zero delay means eligible later, not immediate.

Rendering is an opportunity, not a guaranteed paint after every task. Long synchronous work or an endlessly replenished microtask queue can prevent a visible update. In an interview, state that this example runs as one browser task; do not mix in Node.js-specific scheduling rules.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D'));
console.log('E'); // A E C D B
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Saying setTimeout(fn, 0) executes before promises or guarantees an immediate repaint.

Prove your answer

Run the snippet in a browser and compare the log with a Performance recording.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy can recursively calling queueMicrotask freeze a loading spinner?
DocumentationMDN: Tasks and microtasks ↗
Question #001
My notes & example from experience
002JavaScript/FoundationWhy does every delayed callback show the same index?
The interview scenario

A loop creates three callbacks with var i. All three later log 3 instead of 0, 1, and 2.

How to answer

The callbacks close over the same function-scoped binding, not a frozen copy of its value. By the time the timers execute, the loop has finished and that binding contains 3. A for loop with let creates a separate per-iteration binding.

Closures are useful for private state and callback factories, but they also keep reachable objects alive. For a real UI, ask whether the callback should observe a changing value or preserve the value associated with a particular item.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
} // 0, 1, 2
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Claiming all closures snapshot values when they are created.

Prove your answer

Compare var and let versions, then reorder the input array and check item identity.

The interviewer goes deeperHow is a stale React render closure different from a mutable shared binding?
DocumentationMDN: Closures ↗
Question #002
My notes & example from experience
003JavaScript/FoundationWhy does typeof sometimes throw?
The interview scenario

A developer moves a let declaration lower in a function, and typeof config now throws a ReferenceError.

How to answer

A lexical binding exists throughout its scope but is uninitialized before its declaration executes. That interval is the temporal dead zone. Accessing that binding, even through typeof, throws. By contrast, typeof a truly undeclared name returns "undefined".

Prefer declarations close to their first use, avoid shadowing important outer names, and distinguish initialization from assignment. const prevents rebinding; it does not make the contents of an object immutable.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
function demo() {
  console.log(typeof missing); // "undefined"
  console.log(typeof config);  // ReferenceError
  let config = {};
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Explaining let as simply "not hoisted" without addressing the uninitialized binding.

Prove your answer

Run the function rather than reusing an interactive console scope.

The interviewer goes deeperWhat happens when an inner let shadows an outer variable?
DocumentationMDN: let and temporal dead zones ↗
Question #003
My notes & example from experience
004JavaScript/FoundationA method loses this when passed as a callback
The interview scenario

Passing account.getName directly to a callback API stops reading account.name correctly.

How to answer

For an ordinary function, this depends on how the function is invoked. Extracting a method does not preserve its receiver. Bind it explicitly or pass a wrapper that calls the method on its owner. Arrow functions instead capture this from their surrounding lexical scope.

Choose deliberately: a wrapper can use the current method at invocation time, while bind fixes a function and receiver. Bound functions also have their own identity, which matters when removing event listeners.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const account = { name: 'Nitesh', getName() { return this.name; } };
const readName = account.getName.bind(account);
console.log(readName()); // Nitesh
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Using an arrow as an object method and expecting the object to become its this.

Prove your answer

Test a direct call, detached call, and bound call in strict mode.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy will removeEventListener fail if you call bind again during cleanup?
DocumentationMDN: this ↗
Question #004
My notes & example from experience
005JavaScript/SeniorChoose Promise.all or Promise.allSettled
The interview scenario

A dashboard loads a profile, invoices, and an optional recommendation widget. One request fails.

How to answer

Use Promise.all when the result is useful only if every dependency succeeds; it rejects when one input rejects. Use allSettled for independently useful panels and inspect each status. Both preserve input order in their result arrays, not completion order.

Neither method cancels underlying work automatically. Define required versus optional data, show a local failure state, and use explicit cancellation when the page becomes irrelevant. Do not silently turn an authentication failure into an empty invoice list.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
  loadProfile(), loadInvoices(), loadRecommendations()
]);
const panels = results.map(r =>
  r.status === 'fulfilled' ? r.value : { error: r.reason }
);
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Assuming a rejected Promise.all cancels the other fetches.

Prove your answer

Force each request to fail independently and assert the correct panel behavior.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you cancel remaining work after a required dependency fails?
DocumentationMDN: Promise.all ↗MDN: Promise.allSettled ↗
Question #005
My notes & example from experience
006JavaScript/SeniorRemove an unnecessary request waterfall
The interview scenario

Three independent HTTP calls each take roughly 300 ms, but initial loading takes roughly 900 ms.

How to answer

Start independent operations before awaiting their results, then join them. Sequential awaits serialize work unnecessarily. In the simplified example, parallel elapsed time approaches the slowest request plus overhead rather than the sum.

Do not parallelize real dependencies, and do not equate network concurrency with CPU parallelism. Browser connection limits, server rate limits, contention, and parsing still matter. Bound concurrency when the list is large and collect a network trace before claiming an improvement.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const profilePromise = loadProfile();
const settingsPromise = loadSettings();
const [profile, settings] = await Promise.all([
  profilePromise, settingsPromise
]);
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Wrapping CPU-heavy synchronous functions in Promise.all and expecting multiple CPU cores.

Prove your answer

Inspect request start times and compare cold-load p75 latency.

The interviewer goes deeperWhich calls cannot start before the authenticated user is known?
DocumentationMDN: Promise.all ↗
Question #006
My notes & example from experience
007JavaScript/SeniorA stale search response replaces a newer result
The interview scenario

A user types "react", then "react hooks". The older request finishes last and overwrites the results.

How to answer

Associate each request with an increasing generation number and commit only the latest generation. Also abort the previous fetch to avoid unnecessary work. The generation check protects later asynchronous work that may not honor an abort signal.

Handle HTTP failures explicitly and treat cancellation differently from an actual error. Keep the displayed query associated with its results so loading and stale states are understandable. Debouncing reduces requests but does not, on its own, eliminate this race.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
let generation = 0;
let controller;
async function search(query) {
  const mine = ++generation;
  controller?.abort();
  controller = new AbortController();
  try {
    const r = await fetch('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(query), {
      signal: controller.signal
    });
    if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`);
    const data = await r.json();
    if (mine === generation) renderResults(data);
  } catch (e) {
    if (mine === generation && e.name !== 'AbortError') showError(e);
  }
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Treating debounce as a correctness fix for out-of-order responses.

Prove your answer

Artificially delay A longer than B and verify that B remains displayed.

The interviewer goes deeperWhat changes when results are cached per query?
DocumentationMDN: AbortController ↗
Question #007
My notes & example from experience
008JavaScript/FoundationImplement a cancellable trailing debounce
The interview scenario

An autocomplete should wait until typing pauses, and it must not fire after the view is destroyed.

How to answer

A trailing debounce resets one timer after every call and invokes the function only after a quiet interval. Preserve the latest arguments and receiver, and expose cancel for teardown. Debounce the expensive side effect, not the immediate input value.

Define product behavior before implementing leading execution, trailing execution, maxWait, or flushing on submit. This small implementation intentionally supports trailing calls and cancellation only. Pair it with cancellation or a generation guard for asynchronous responses.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timer;
  function debounced(...args) {
    const receiver = this;
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(receiver, args), delay);
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer);
  return debounced;
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Recreating the debounced function on every render, which creates independent timers.

Prove your answer

Use fake timers to check rapid calls, the final arguments, and cancel before expiry.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy might autosave need maxWait while search does not?

Question #008
My notes & example from experience
009JavaScript/SeniorThrottle, debounce, or requestAnimationFrame?
The interview scenario

A scroll handler updates a progress bar and also sends analytics events. Should both use the same timing strategy?

How to answer

Use requestAnimationFrame to coalesce visual work with a rendering opportunity, keeping at most one pending callback. Use a separately defined throttle for periodic analytics and debounce for work that should wait until activity stops. These are different contracts.

A scroll event may already occur near frame frequency, so measure the actual saved work. Keep the handler lightweight, avoid repeated synchronous layout reads, and do not rely on animation frames for background-tab delivery guarantees.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
let pending = false;
function onScroll() {
  if (pending) return;
  pending = true;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    pending = false;
    updateProgress(window.scrollY);
  });
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Assuming requestAnimationFrame always runs at 60 Hz or always reduces scroll-event frequency.

Prove your answer

Profile a long scroll on a high-refresh display and in a background tab.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you guarantee a final analytics sample when scrolling stops?
DocumentationMDN: addEventListener ↗
Question #009
My notes & example from experience
010JavaScript/FoundationWhy did copying an object still mutate the original?
The interview scenario

Updating copy.preferences.theme also changes the original profile even though copy was made with object spread.

How to answer

Object spread copies the outer object, but nested references remain shared. Copy every changed level for an immutable update. structuredClone can copy supported graphs, including cycles, but is not a universal clone for functions, DOM nodes, or arbitrary class behavior.

Use structural sharing for frequently updated application state so unchanged branches retain identity. Deep cloning the entire state tree is often unnecessary work and defeats useful referential equality. JSON serialization also changes or rejects several JavaScript value types.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const next = {
  ...profile,
  preferences: { ...profile.preferences, theme: 'dark' }
};
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Claiming the spread operator creates a deep copy.

Prove your answer

Freeze the original in a test and assert that only the edited path has new references.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy can cloning all state make memoized children slower?
DocumentationMDN: structuredClone ↗
Question #010
My notes & example from experience
011JavaScript/FoundationSorting unexpectedly changes another component
The interview scenario

A child sorts its items prop. A sibling suddenly shows the same reordered list.

How to answer

Array.sort mutates its receiver. Use toSorted where supported, or copy before sorting, when the input belongs to a parent or shared cache. Provide a numeric comparator for numeric data; default sorting compares string representations.

The copy is shallow, so item objects remain shared. Avoid writing into those objects while sorting. Decide how ties, missing values, locale-sensitive text, and deterministic server/client ordering should behave.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const ranked = items.toSorted((a, b) => b.score - a.score);
// Compatibility alternative:
const rankedCopy = [...items].sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Fixing the array copy but still mutating each item during the comparator.

Prove your answer

Assert the original order is unchanged and test 2, 10, and missing values.

The interviewer goes deeperHow could locale-dependent sorting create a hydration mismatch?
DocumentationMDN: toSorted ↗
Question #011
My notes & example from experience
012JavaScript/SeniorWhen should a keyed lookup use Map?
The interview scenario

A UI repeatedly finds users by ID inside a render loop, producing noticeably slow large lists.

How to answer

Build a lookup once per relevant data version rather than repeatedly scanning the same array. Map supports arbitrary keys and insertion-order iteration; a plain object can be appropriate for string-keyed records with a carefully chosen shape.

Avoid promising a language-guaranteed O(1) implementation: Map requires average sublinear access. In typical usage, eliminating repeated linear scans is the important improvement. Normalization also creates a synchronization responsibility when the source collection changes.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const byId = new Map(users.map(user => [user.id, user]));
const visible = selectedIds.map(id => byId.get(id)).filter(Boolean);
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Building the entire lookup again for every individual row.

Prove your answer

Benchmark realistic list sizes and include construction cost.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you handle duplicate IDs or preserve display order?
DocumentationMDN: Map ↗
Question #012
My notes & example from experience
013JavaScript/FoundationWhy does zero disappear when applying a default?
The interview scenario

A volume setting of 0 becomes 50, and a valid empty string is replaced by placeholder text.

How to answer

The logical OR operator falls back for every falsy value, including 0, false, and the empty string. The ?? operator falls back only for null or undefined. Choose the operator according to the domain, not habit.

Optional chaining stops a nullish property access but does not validate the resulting value. For example, a server may send a string where a number is required. Validate boundary data separately and preserve meaningful false or zero states.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const volume = settings.volume ?? 50;
const label = response.user?.displayName ?? 'Guest';
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Treating optional chaining as schema validation.

Prove your answer

Test null, undefined, 0, false, empty text, and malformed values.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy is mixing ?? with || without parentheses a syntax error?
DocumentationMDN: Nullish coalescing ↗
Question #013
My notes & example from experience
014JavaScript/FoundationDelegate events for a changing list
The interview scenario

A table adds and removes thousands of rows. Attaching separate listeners to every delete button is cumbersome.

How to answer

Attach one listener to a stable ancestor and inspect the event target to find the closest matching control. Check that the matched element belongs to the intended container. Event bubbling allows newly inserted descendants to work without additional listeners.

Account for nested interactive elements, stopped propagation, and Shadow DOM retargeting where relevant. Prefer actual buttons for keyboard activation. Delegation simplifies listener ownership; it does not replace semantic HTML or authorization.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
list.addEventListener('click', event => {
  if (!(event.target instanceof Element)) return;
  const button = event.target.closest('button[data-remove]');
  if (!button || !list.contains(button)) return;
  removeItem(button.dataset.remove);
});
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Using event.target.dataset directly when the click actually lands on a nested icon.

Prove your answer

Click text, icon, and keyboard-activated buttons, including dynamically inserted rows.

The interviewer goes deeperWhich events do not bubble in the way this pattern requires?
DocumentationMDN: addEventListener ↗
Question #014
My notes & example from experience
015JavaScript/SeniorA page gets slower after repeated navigation
The interview scenario

After opening and closing a live dashboard many times, duplicate updates appear and memory keeps growing.

How to answer

Look for resources whose lifetime exceeds their owner: listeners, timers, subscriptions, workers, observers, or retained detached DOM. Provide symmetrical teardown and verify that callback identity matches the registered listener. An AbortSignal can group supported event-listener cleanup.

Garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects, not everything no longer visible. A closure reachable from a global listener can retain an entire component-related object graph. Use heap snapshots and repeated navigation, not a single memory reading, to validate the fix.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const controller = new AbortController();
window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal: controller.signal });
// During teardown:
controller.abort();
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Assuming the browser frees every listener when a component disappears.

Prove your answer

Perform 30 mount/unmount cycles and compare listener counts and retained heap paths.

The interviewer goes deeperWhich resources need explicit cleanup even when DOM nodes are removed?

Question #015
My notes & example from experience
016JavaScript/SeniorWhen does WeakMap help with memory?
The interview scenario

A utility stores measurements for DOM nodes in a global Map. Removed nodes remain retained.

How to answer

WeakMap allows object keys to be collected when nothing else strongly references them. It is useful for metadata whose lifetime should follow an object. It is not an iterable cache and does not provide deterministic garbage-collection notifications.

Check for other references to the same nodes before blaming the container. For a cache keyed by strings or one that needs eviction metrics, use an explicit bounded Map with a lifetime policy instead. Weak references are not a substitute for unsubscribing listeners or stopping timers.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const measurements = new WeakMap();
function remember(node) {
  measurements.set(node, node.getBoundingClientRect());
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Using WeakMap for string IDs or expecting a size property and reliable enumeration.

Prove your answer

Inspect retained paths rather than asserting when garbage collection must happen.

The interviewer goes deeperWhy should a request-result cache usually have explicit limits?
DocumentationMDN: WeakMap ↗
Question #016
My notes & example from experience
017JavaScript/SeniorMove a CPU-heavy calculation off the main thread
The interview scenario

A local CSV analysis blocks typing for two seconds even though no network request is involved.

How to answer

Use a Web Worker for substantial CPU work that does not require direct DOM access. Send input and receive results through messages. Include a job ID so stale results are ignored, and terminate or cancel obsolete work according to the worker protocol.

Message serialization and copying can be expensive; transferable buffers can avoid copying supported data but detach ownership from the sender. Workers do not make DOM updates parallel. For small work, chunking on the main thread may cost less than managing a worker.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./analysis.js', import.meta.url), {
  type: 'module'
});
worker.postMessage({ jobId: 7, rows });
worker.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  if (data.jobId === currentJobId) showResult(data.result);
};
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Converting a calculation into an async function and claiming it now runs off-thread.

Prove your answer

Compare interaction latency, transfer overhead, and total completion time.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you cancel a worker job without destroying reusable worker state?
DocumentationMDN: Using Web Workers ↗
Question #017
My notes & example from experience
018JavaScript/Senior/Check browser supportYield during long work without starving rendering
The interview scenario

A loop awaits Promise.resolve every hundred items, yet the interface still feels frozen.

How to answer

Awaiting an already resolved promise resumes via microtasks, which can continue before rendering. Split work into small bounded chunks and yield to the scheduler when available, with a task-based fallback for unsupported browsers.

Choose a chunk budget from measured work rather than assuming every item costs the same. A worker is often better for sustained CPU processing. Cancellation must be checked between chunks, and the user should receive useful progress without excessive DOM updates.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
async function yieldToBrowser() {
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) await scheduler.yield();
  else await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  processItem(items[i]);
  if (i % 100 === 99) await yieldToBrowser();
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Assuming every await gives the browser a chance to paint.

Prove your answer

Inspect long tasks and type in a text field while the calculation runs.

The interviewer goes deeperWhat happens to the fallback timer in a background tab?
DocumentationMDN: scheduler.yield ↗MDN: Tasks and microtasks ↗
Question #018
My notes & example from experience
019JavaScript/FoundationWhy does async forEach finish too early?
The interview scenario

After await records.forEach(async ...) the UI announces success before any saves finish.

How to answer

forEach ignores callback return values and returns undefined. Awaiting that return does not await the promises created inside the callbacks. Use for...of with await for intentional sequential work, or map to promises and await their aggregate for bounded-sized independent work.

Choose ordering and failure behavior explicitly. Large batches need a concurrency limit rather than launching every save together. A failed aggregate also needs an error policy; do not announce success if only part of a required workflow completed.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
// Sequential:
for (const record of records) await save(record);
// Concurrent, only for a suitably small independent batch:
await Promise.all(records.map(record => save(record)));
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Adding async to the outer function without changing the iteration pattern.

Prove your answer

Use delayed fake saves and assert that completion occurs after the required results.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you stop a sequential batch after cancellation?
DocumentationMDN: Promise.all ↗
Question #019
My notes & example from experience
020JavaScript/LeadLimit concurrency for hundreds of requests
The interview scenario

A bulk preview starts 500 fetches at once and triggers rate limits and large memory spikes.

How to answer

Keep a fixed number of workers consuming a shared queue. Preserve input order in a separate result array and decide whether a failure stops scheduling or is collected. Bound both concurrency and total work; a concurrency cap is not the same as a requests-per-second limit.

The illustrative pool below records individual outcomes rather than failing fast. Production code should add cancellation, retry budgets, and backoff only where operations are safe to retry. Validate the limit so zero workers cannot silently produce empty results.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
async function pool(items, limit, task) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(limit) || limit < 1) throw new RangeError('limit');
  const out = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  async function worker() {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;
      try { out[i] = { ok: true, value: await task(items[i], i) }; }
      catch (error) { out[i] = { ok: false, error }; }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  return out;
}
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Using Promise.all on the full input and adding delays only after requests already started.

Prove your answer

Instrument active requests and assert that the maximum never exceeds the limit.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would a server Retry-After response affect your queue?
DocumentationMDN: Promise.all ↗MDN: Promise.allSettled ↗
Question #020
My notes & example from experience
021JavaScript/SeniorSplit a large feature with dynamic import
The interview scenario

A rarely used chart editor adds substantial JavaScript to the initial route.

How to answer

Dynamic import can defer loading and evaluating a module until the feature is needed. Keep imports statically understandable to the bundler and inspect the production output; an import boundary alone does not guarantee an ideal chunk.

Handle loading and import failure, and consider preloading on likely user intent. Splitting everything into tiny chunks can create overhead and waterfalls. Tree shaking also depends on module structure and side-effect declarations, not merely using named imports.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
async function openEditor() {
  showLoading();
  try {
    const { mountEditor } = await import('./chart-editor.js');
    mountEditor(document.querySelector('#editor'));
  } catch (error) { showRetry(error); }
}

Common mistake

Claiming that every named import or barrel import is automatically cheap.

Prove your answer

Question #021
My notes & example from experience
022JavaScript/LeadA cyclic module import fails only during startup
The interview scenario

Two modules import each other. A top-level read sometimes produces an uninitialized-binding error.

How to answer

ES module imports are live bindings, not copied snapshots. Cycles can be valid, but reading a binding before its exporting module initializes it can fail. Top-level initialization order becomes part of the problem.

Break the cycle by extracting shared contracts or utilities into a third module, or move an operation behind a function called after initialization. Avoid hiding the problem with arbitrary timers. Top-level await can further complicate dependency sequencing and should be used with a clear loading contract.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
// constants.js: shared dependency, no feature imports
export const DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE = 25;
// list.js and pagination.js both import constants.js
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Assuming imports execute top to bottom exactly like textual concatenation.

Prove your answer

Test a clean page load, not only hot-module replacement.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you enforce acyclic feature boundaries in a large repository?

Question #022
My notes & example from experience
023JavaScript/SeniorDo not trust JSON just because TypeScript accepts it
The interview scenario

A frontend casts an API response to User. Production crashes when name is null instead of a string.

How to answer

Type assertions do not validate runtime data. Parse untrusted values at the boundary, validate the fields the UI requires, and map them into an internal model. Keep malformed-response failures distinct from empty-state results.

Use a maintained schema validator for complex contracts or focused checks for a small shape. Consider schema versioning and tolerant handling of optional additions. Avoid logging sensitive payloads when reporting validation errors.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
function parseUser(value) {
  if (!value || typeof value !== 'object' ||
      typeof value.id !== 'string' || typeof value.name !== 'string') {
    throw new TypeError('Invalid user response');
  }
  return { id: value.id, name: value.name };
}

Question #023
My notes & example from experience
024JavaScript/SeniorRepresent async UI as explicit states
The interview scenario

A form combines isLoading, hasError, and isSuccess booleans and occasionally displays contradictory messages.

How to answer

Model mutually exclusive phases as a discriminated state: idle, submitting, success, or error, with the data required by each phase. Define allowed transitions and keep a submission identity so an old completion cannot overwrite a newer attempt.

Not every component needs a state-machine library. A reducer or tagged union can make the contract clear. The important part is preventing impossible combinations and specifying cancellation, retry, and unmount behavior rather than adding more flags.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
// TypeScript: exactly one phase at a time
type SaveState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'submitting'; requestId: number }
  | { status: 'success'; savedId: string }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string };
Framework examples are fragments; app helpers and setup may be omitted. Only the Visual Labs execute demonstrations.
Common mistake

Question #024
My notes & example from experience
025React/FoundationWhy do three increments increase state only once?
The interview scenario

A handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times, but the count rises by one.

How to answer

Each handler sees the state snapshot from the render that created it. All three expressions compute the same replacement value. Functional updaters are queued transformations, so each receives the pending result of the previous update.

Keep updater functions pure: React may invoke them more than once in development checks. Batching reduces commits; it does not mutate the variable captured by the current handler. Separate user interactions still have their own event boundaries.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);

Expecting console.log(count) immediately after setCount to print the next render value.

My notes & example from experience
026React/FoundationA state update does not repaint the UI
The interview scenario

A handler mutates user.name and calls setUser(user), but the displayed name remains unchanged.

How to answer

Treat state as immutable and create a new object for the changed path. Reusing the same reference can let React skip an update because the new value compares equal with Object.is. Mutation also alters objects held by earlier render snapshots.

Copy only the levels that changed, or use a well-understood immutable-update helper. Do not use forced rerenders to hide ownership bugs. Keep derived values out of state unless there is a real independent lifecycle.

Question #026
My notes & example from experience
027React/FoundationInput values move to the wrong row after sorting
The interview scenario

A list uses array indexes as keys. After sorting, edited input state appears under a different person.

How to answer

React associates state with component type, tree position, and keys within the parent. Stable entity keys let identity follow the item rather than its old position. Index keys can misassociate local state when insertion, deletion, or reordering changes the list.

Use a different key deliberately when you want a form reset, such as switching from one customer to another. Do not generate keys randomly during render: that destroys continuity and causes remounts. Keys are not a global identifier and are not passed as a normal prop.

If a value is fully determined by current props and state, derive it during render. The Effect adds another render and temporarily leaves two representations out of sync. Use memoization only when a measured expensive calculation benefits from reuse.

Effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not for every calculation. Event-specific work belongs in the event handler. Keeping one source of truth also makes transitions, server rendering, and tests easier to reason about.

A new object identity appears on each render, so React sees a changed dependency. Prefer constructing that object inside the Effect and depending on the primitive values that actually control the connection. Include all reactive dependencies instead of disabling the linter.

The interval callback captured the count from its initial render. When the update depends only on previous state, pass a functional updater instead of reading that captured value. Always clear the interval during cleanup.

Strict Mode adds development-only checks, including extra rendering and Effect or ref setup/cleanup checks in applicable configurations. These help expose impure rendering and missing cleanup. They are not evidence that production must execute every Effect twice.

Fix the lifecycle so setup followed by cleanup followed by setup leaves the application correct. Do not suppress setup with a global "already ran" flag. Mutations such as purchases should be initiated from deliberate user actions and protected by server-side idempotency where needed.

Question #031
My notes & example from experience
032React/SeniorA render happened, but no DOM changed
The interview scenario

Render counters increase during interaction, yet the DOM looks unchanged. Is every render a performance bug?

How to answer

Rendering computes a possible UI; committing applies the selected changes. React may render work that produces no DOM difference or work that is interrupted and discarded. Keep render functions pure because execution does not guarantee a commit.

Measure expensive committed work, interaction latency, and browser layout or paint before optimizing counts. Mutating external state or sending analytics during render is unsafe. Place user-action analytics in event handlers and lifecycle synchronization in Effects as appropriate.

My notes & example from experience
033React/SeniorWhy did memo not stop a child from rendering?

How to answer

memo compares props with Object.is by default. Newly created object and function references differ even when they represent the same intent. Stabilize only values that affect a measured expensive boundary, or move the state that changes so the parent does less work.

A child still rerenders for its own state or context changes. Custom comparisons can cost more than rendering and must account for callbacks, whose closures may change. useCallback preserves a function reference; it does not prevent the function from being created conceptually or make its body faster.

How to answer

React Compiler can automatically memoize eligible React code when it is configured in the build. It does not fix slow network calls, huge DOM trees, blocking browser work, or incorrect state ownership. Follow the Rules of React and inspect compatibility diagnostics.

Adopt it incrementally, benchmark representative interactions, and avoid mass-removing existing memoization before validating behavior. Compiler support in a framework does not imply every project has enabled it. Correctness must not depend on a memoized value being retained forever.

Consumers subscribe to the context value, not automatically to individual object fields. Split contexts by ownership and update frequency, keep provider values stable when unchanged, or use a suitable selector-based external store for frequent granular updates.

Context distributes a value; it is not a full server-data cache. Avoid making every state global. Moving a provider closer to its consumers can reduce scope, while ordinary component composition may eliminate the need for context entirely.

Question #035
My notes & example from experience
036React/FoundationChoose controlled or uncontrolled inputs
The interview scenario

A large form is slow, and an input warns that it changed from uncontrolled to controlled.

How to answer

A controlled input receives its current value from React and updates it synchronously in onChange. An uncontrolled input uses the DOM as its source of truth, often with defaultValue and FormData or refs at submission. Do not switch ownership mid-lifecycle.

Initialize controlled text values to an empty string rather than undefined. Keep urgent input state local and move expensive dependents behind an appropriate boundary. Choose a form library based on validation, subscriptions, accessibility, and field count, not on a claim that one pattern is always faster.

Question #036
My notes & example from experience
037React/SeniorWhy does Suspense not catch my Effect fetch?
The interview scenario

A component fetches data inside useEffect, but a surrounding Suspense fallback never appears.

How to answer

Suspense responds to supported resources read during rendering, such as lazy-loaded code or a compatible promise/data integration. An Effect starts after rendering and does not automatically suspend the component. Use explicit loading state or the framework or library integration designed for Suspense.

Place boundaries around meaningful user-visible units, not every small element. They define loading and reveal behavior, not arbitrary request concurrency. Add error boundaries for rejection and think about preserving already useful content during updates.

Question #037
My notes & example from experience
038React/SeniorWhat does an Error Boundary actually catch?
The interview scenario

A widget crash should not blank the page, but a failed click-handler request is not caught by its boundary.

How to answer

Error boundaries isolate errors during rendering and relevant React lifecycle work below them. They do not generally catch event-handler errors, arbitrary asynchronous callbacks, or every server-rendering failure. Handle expected request failures where they occur and render a useful state.

Choose a boundary per recoverable product area and log sanitized diagnostics. A retry should address the failing resource, not merely render the same broken state again. Framework-specific server error handling has its own recovery contract.

Question #038
My notes & example from experience
039React/SeniorKeep urgent input separate from a Transition
The interview scenario

Switching a tab causes an expensive React tree update and makes typing or clicking feel delayed.

How to answer

Mark the non-urgent state update as a Transition so React can prioritize urgent work and interrupt eligible rendering. Keep the state controlling a text input urgent. A Transition is scheduling, not a time delay and not a worker.

Expensive synchronous calculations executed directly inside the callback still block. Move CPU work to a better data structure or worker, and handle asynchronous response ordering separately. Show pending feedback that preserves useful existing content rather than needlessly replacing everything.

Question #039
My notes & example from experience
040React/SenioruseDeferredValue is not a network debounce
The interview scenario

A result list should lag behind the input when rendering is expensive, but the API must not be called for every character.

How to answer

useDeferredValue lets a less urgent subtree use a deferred version of a value while urgent UI updates first. It does not specify a fixed waiting interval and does not inherently reduce requests. Debounce or otherwise control the data-fetch trigger separately when needed.

The expensive subtree usually needs a memoization boundary or compatible cached resources for deferral to help. Show stale-content feedback, and remember that deferred rendering is different from suppressing intermediate queries. Preserve cancellation and response-order protection.

Question #040
My notes & example from experience
041React/LeadSubscribe safely to a non-React store
The interview scenario

A custom store is read directly during render and subscribed to in an Effect. Concurrent rendering sometimes displays inconsistent values.

How to answer

useSyncExternalStore provides the subscription and snapshot contract React needs for external mutable stores. getSnapshot must return a stable snapshot while the store has not changed, and subscribe must return an unsubscribe function. Supply a compatible server snapshot when server rendering is used.

Do not return a brand-new object on every getSnapshot call. Keep subscriptions stable and make updates observable. This solves React integration; it does not design the store, normalize data, or create selector granularity for you.

const count = useSyncExternalStore(
  counterStore.subscribe,
  counterStore.getSnapshot,
  counterStore.getServerSnapshot
);

Question #041

The interview scenario

A form needs a pending state and a server-validated result without scattered submission flags.

How to answer

useActionState connects an action to its latest returned state and exposes a pending indicator. The action receives the previous state before its submitted payload, which changes the expected function signature. A server action must still authenticate, authorize, and validate. Hook state is not a security boundary. Preserve form fields appropriately after errors and provide accessible feedback for pending, success, and failure states.

Question #042

043React/Senior/React 19+Why is useFormStatus always not pending?
The interview scenario

A component calls useFormStatus and then returns the form whose submission it wants to observe.

How to answer

useFormStatus reads the status of an enclosing parent form. It cannot observe a form created below the component making the call. Put the status-reading submit button inside that form as a descendant component.

Use the returned pending state for feedback and prevent accidental repeated interaction, while keeping the server safe against duplicate requests. Nested forms are invalid HTML, so composition should preserve one clear form owner.

Question #043
My notes & example from experience
044React/Senior/React 19+Make optimistic updates reversible and ordered
The interview scenario

A user likes an item immediately, but the server rejects the change or two rapid toggles finish out of order.

How to answer

Optimistic state is a temporary prediction layered over authoritative state. useOptimistic helps render that prediction during an Action, but your mutation protocol still needs stable IDs, validation, error feedback, and ordering or reconciliation.

Design rollback for the actual interaction: one failed update must not erase a later successful action. For counts or toggles, a server-returned canonical version is often safer than guessing final state. Avoid optimism for irreversible or high-consequence operations unless the experience can clearly communicate uncertainty.

const [optimisticLiked, setOptimisticLiked] = useOptimistic(liked);
async function likeAction() {
  setOptimisticLiked(true);
  const canonical = await saveLike();
  setLiked(canonical.liked);
}
// Invoke as a form Action or inside startTransition;
// surface rejection and reconcile authoritative state.

Question #044

045React/Senior/React 19+Read a promise with use without recreating it forever
The interview scenario

A Client Component calls use(fetchData()) during every render and repeatedly suspends.

How to answer

use reads a supported resource during render; pending promises suspend and rejected promises reach an error boundary. The promise must be stable across retries and rerenders through a compatible cache or a promise passed from an appropriate parent or server integration.

Unlike ordinary Hooks, use can be called conditionally, but it still belongs inside a component or Hook and not inside try/catch. For Server Components, async/await is often the clearer option. Do not build an unbounded global cache that mixes users just to stabilize promises.

Question #045

046React/Senior/React 19+Expose a small imperative ref API

How to answer

In React 19, function components can receive ref as a prop. Use useImperativeHandle to expose the minimal operations the parent needs, such as focus or selecting text, rather than leaking an entire implementation. Older supported React versions may require forwardRef.

Prefer props for declarative state such as open or selected. An imperative handle is useful for browser actions that do not map cleanly to a state value. Ref changes do not trigger rendering, so do not use a ref as the only storage for visible UI state.

Question #049
My notes & example from experience
050React/Senior/React 19.2+Preserve tab state with Activity
The interview scenario

A tab should keep its draft and DOM state while hidden, without leaving its active subscriptions running.

How to answer

Activity can hide a subtree while preserving its state and DOM, and clean up its Effects while hidden. When visible again, Effects are recreated. This differs from removing the subtree, which discards its local state, or merely adding display:none, which does not provide React lifecycle management.

Preserved DOM consumes memory. Choose which tabs are worth retaining, verify focus behavior, and test components that assume mount means visible. Hidden activity is not a security boundary; sensitive data must still be governed by session and authorization rules.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
<Activity mode={activeTab === 'editor' ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>
  <Editor />
</Activity>

Assuming hiding with ordinary CSS automatically unsubscribes React Effects.

Question #050
My notes & example from experience
051React/Senior/React 19.2+Read fresh Effect logic without reconnecting
The interview scenario

A connection depends on roomId, but its connected notification should always use the latest theme.

How to answer

useEffectEvent extracts non-reactive logic called from an Effect or an Effect-owned callback. It can read current props and state without making that logic a reason to resynchronize the connection. Keep true connection dependencies in the Effect.

It is not a universal dependency escape hatch and should not be passed around as an ordinary event handler. If changing a value must recreate the external connection, that value remains a dependency. Follow the current lint rules and keep the event declaration near its owning Effect.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => notify(theme));
useEffect(() => {
  const connection = connect(roomId);
  connection.on('connected', () => onConnected());
  return () => connection.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);

Wrapping the entire Effect in an Effect Event just to remove dependencies.

Question #051
My notes & example from experience
052React/Senior/React 19.3+Use ViewTransition without delaying urgent feedback
The interview scenario

A product detail panel should animate entering and exiting, while typing and immediate feedback remain responsive.

How to answer

React 19.3 stabilizes ViewTransition for coordinating eligible DOM changes with the browser View Transition API. Wrap the relevant region and use a Transition for the state change. Urgent updates are not automatically turned into animated transitions.

Treat animation as progressive enhancement: support reduced motion, avoid animating every loading fallback, and keep stable identity where shared transitions are intended. Framework-bundled React versions and browser capabilities still need checking. An animation does not make a slow request complete sooner.

<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setOpen(v => !v))}>

</button>

Question #052
My notes & example from experience
053React/Senior/React 19.3+Use Fragment refs without adding a wrapper element
The interview scenario

A reusable component needs to focus a group of siblings, but adding a div breaks the surrounding grid.

How to answer

React 19.3 supports refs on an explicit Fragment. The ref exposes a FragmentInstance with supported group operations, such as focusing descendants, observing relevant children, and measuring rectangles. It is not a real DOM element or an unrestricted replacement for HTMLElement.

Use the explicit Fragment syntax because the short fragment form cannot receive a ref. Prefer normal semantic grouping when the content requires a landmark or heading relationship. Removing a wrapper for layout convenience should not remove necessary semantics.

</Fragment>

Question #053
My notes & example from experience
054React/Senior/React 19.3+Render a browser-only region with use(browser())
The interview scenario

A small widget depends on the browser local timezone and cannot provide meaningful matching server content.

How to answer

In React 19.3, use(browser()) suspends during server rendering and proceeds in the browser. Put the component under Suspense so the server can render a useful fallback. In an RSC application, call it from a Client Component, not a Server Component.

This is an explicit server-rendering opt-out for a region, not a general hydration-error repair. Prefer deterministic server-rendered content when possible. Browser-only does not mean import-time access to window is safe in every build pipeline, and the actual bundled React runtime must support the API.

import { browser } from 'react-dom';
function LocalZone() {
  use(browser());
  return <p>{Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone}</p>;
}
// Parent: <Suspense fallback={<p>Local timezone loading...</p>}>
//           <LocalZone />
//         </Suspense>

Question #054
My notes & example from experience

The interview scenario

You are building a public catalog, an authenticated account page, and a highly interactive editor. Should all three render the same way?

Server Components describe where components execute and what code ships, not simply whether HTML is generated at build time or request time. Question #055

056Next.js/Senior/App RouterPut the client boundary as low as practical
The interview scenario

A page imports a chart with event handlers. Adding use client to the root makes the client bundle much larger.

How to answer

Keep server-only data access and non-interactive rendering in Server Components. Add use client at the module boundary that needs state, Effects, event handlers, or browser APIs. Modules imported through that boundary join the client graph as applicable.

Client Components can still participate in server-generated initial HTML; use client does not mean "never runs on the server." Pass serializable data and compose server-rendered content through slots rather than importing server-only modules into a client file. Measure the resulting bundle, not just file size.

Question #056
My notes & example from experience
057Next.js/Senior/SSR / App RouterDiagnose a hydration mismatch instead of hiding it
The interview scenario

A page renders the current time, a random ID, and browser-specific theme markup. Hydration produces warnings.

How to answer

Hydration expects the initial client output to match the server HTML. Make that first render deterministic: pass a serialized timestamp or ID, use a stable fallback for browser-only data, and keep markup valid. Check locale, timezone, extensions, and invalid nesting as well.

Use client alone does not disable server rendering. Suppressing a warning is a narrow escape hatch, not a repair for a structurally different tree. Deliberately isolate browser-only regions only when there is no useful server representation.

Question #058
My notes & example from experience
059Next.js/Lead/Compare configured cache modelsName the cache before explaining a stale response
The interview scenario

A database row is updated, but the browser still shows old data. The team says "Next.js cached it" without identifying where.

How to answer

Trace the full path: browser HTTP cache, CDN, server data or component cache, and client navigation cache. Request-scoped deduplication is different from storage across requests. A refresh of one layer need not invalidate another.

The previous App Router caching model and the opt-in Cache Components model have different APIs and assumptions. Record the exact version, flags, fetch options, key, lifetime, tags, and deployment cache handler. Use per-user cache isolation for protected data rather than assuming every cached response is public-safe.

Claiming every fetch is always cached, or no fetch is ever cached, across all Next.js versions.

Question #059
My notes & example from experience
060Next.js/Senior/Next.js 16+; opt-inUse Cache Components with an explicit lifetime
The interview scenario

A public product summary is expensive to compute, but personalized availability must remain request-specific.

How to answer

With cacheComponents enabled, use cache can retain a function or component result. Set an intentional cacheLife and tags for invalidation. Keep request-specific work outside a public cached scope and stream it under a suitable Suspense boundary.

Do not read cookies or headers directly inside a normal use cache scope. Resolve necessary request values outside and reason carefully about cache keys and authorization before passing arguments. Caching is an explicit freshness and privacy decision, not just a performance annotation.

// next.config.ts: { cacheComponents: true }
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';
async function getPublicProduct(id) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');
  cacheTag(`product:${id}`);
  return readPublicProduct(id);
}

Question #060

An older tutorial reads params.slug and cookies().get directly. The code no longer matches the current App Router contract.

In current Next.js 16 code, treat route params and request APIs such as cookies and headers according to their asynchronous contracts. Await them before reading values. Page searchParams is also asynchronous; the client useSearchParams Hook is a different API.

Reading request-specific values affects how work can be prerendered or streamed, especially with Cache Components. Do not paste an old synchronous snippet into a new project or cast away a type error. Read the docs that match the installed version.

Question #061
My notes & example from experience
062Next.js/Senior/Next.js 16+Choose updateTag or stale-while-revalidate
The interview scenario

After editing a post, its author must see the new value immediately. A public news feed can tolerate briefly stale content.

How to answer

Use updateTag inside a Server Action for read-your-own-writes: tagged entries expire and the next read waits for fresh data. Use revalidateTag(tag, "max") for stale-while-revalidate behavior, where a subsequent visit can receive cached content while refreshing in the background.

updateTag is restricted to Server Actions; revalidateTag is also available in Route Handlers. Assign tags when caching the data, commit the write before invalidating, and avoid the deprecated single-argument revalidateTag pattern. Invalidation is not a broadcast that magically changes every already-open tab.

ILLUSTRATIVE CODE
// Inside an authorized Server Action, after a successful write:
updateTag(`post:${postId}`);
// Different contract, e.g. public feed invalidation:
revalidateTag('public-feed', 'max');

Common mistake

Using updateTag in a webhook Route Handler or assuming max blocks for fresh data.

Prove your answer

Question #062
My notes & example from experience
063Next.js/Senior/App RouterWhy does router.refresh still show stale data?
The interview scenario

A client mutation succeeds, then router.refresh runs, but the old cached total remains visible.

How to answer

router.refresh requests a new Server Component payload and merges it while preserving unaffected client and browser state. It does not invalidate server-side cached data. A new render can therefore read the same cached result.

Invalidate the server cache at the mutation boundary using the appropriate tag or path strategy, then ensure the client receives updated UI. Distinguish refresh from full browser reload and from server cache expiry. A client-only query cache may also need its own invalidation.

await updateSettingsAction(formData); // action invalidates owned cache

How to answer

No. Authenticate the request and authorize the specific operation and resource inside the server-side entry point or a trusted data-access layer. Validate arguments, reject cross-tenant access, and design appropriate rate limiting and audit events.

Client UI restrictions improve experience but do not enforce permissions. Action identifiers and framework protections do not replace authorization. Check ownership at the point of mutation, use transactional or idempotent behavior where needed, and return only data the caller may see.

Question #064

The interview scenario

How to answer

Browser validation is a usability feature and can be bypassed. Read FormData defensively because entries may be strings, Files, or null. Parse and validate the intended schema, authenticate the caller, and return structured field errors for expected failures.

Use useActionState or another clear result contract to show errors without losing useful input. Preserve progressive enhancement where supported, label each field, and associate errors with inputs. Do not send raw database errors or sensitive validation context to the browser.

Question #065
My notes & example from experience
066Next.js/Senior/Next.js 16+What changed from middleware.ts to proxy.ts?
The interview scenario

A migration to Next.js 16 prompts the team to rename middleware. They also want to move all database authorization there.

Next.js 16 uses the proxy naming convention to make the network boundary clearer. Use it for narrowly scoped request redirects, rewrites, or preliminary checks. Configure matchers so static assets and unrelated routes are not processed unnecessarily.

Do not make Proxy the sole protection for data or mutations. Authorization belongs close to protected operations because routes and actions have different entry paths. Check runtime compatibility instead of assuming old middleware runtime behavior remains the right model.

Question #068
My notes & example from experience
069Next.js/Senior/Next.js 16.3+Recover from a failed Server Component region
The interview scenario

A dashboard region fails on the server. Resetting only client error state does not refetch the failed data.

How to answer

Use the framework error conventions for route-level failures and choose a recovery path that can actually rerun the failed server work. Next.js 16.3 adds catchError for custom boundaries; its retry operation refetches and rerenders children, while reset only clears error state without refetching.

The custom boundary is framework-aware, so redirect and notFound control flow are not accidentally swallowed. Keep user-facing errors generic, log diagnostic identifiers, and isolate recoverable regions. Do not expose production stack traces or retry non-idempotent mutations automatically.

Question #072
My notes & example from experience
073Next.js/Senior/App Router; config-sensitivePrerender popular paths without building millions of pages
The interview scenario

A catalog has millions of items, but only a small popular subset should be rendered during the build.

How to answer

generateStaticParams selects dynamic parameter values for build-time work. It is not a live inventory of every path forever and is not rerun automatically as part of ordinary ISR revalidation. Choose how unlisted paths are served and how content is refreshed.

With Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations and the required flags, loading-shell and later prerendering behavior differs from older assumptions. Explain the actual configured model, check deployment support, and avoid caching access-controlled or incorrect availability information as public content.

Question #074

075Next.js/Senior/Next.js 16 image guidanceAn optimized image is still the LCP bottleneck
The interview scenario

How to answer

Image optimization is only part of the path. Provide correct intrinsic dimensions or a stable fill container, an accurate sizes contract, and an intentional loading priority. Do not lazy-load a known critical hero without considering its discovery path.

In Next.js 16, priority is deprecated in favor of clearer preload behavior. The docs also recommend eager loading or fetchPriority in many cases; do not stack preload with conflicting loading strategies. Restrict remotePatterns and measure the actual selected resource, not just the source asset.

Question #076
My notes & example from experience
077Next.js/Lead/Next.jsA secret appears in the browser bundle
The interview scenario

A developer prefixes an upstream API key with NEXT_PUBLIC_ so a Client Component can read it.

How to answer

NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are intended for browser exposure and are typically inlined into client code at build time. Never put secrets there. Keep credentials in server-only modules and expose an authorized, minimal operation through server-side code instead.

A non-public variable can still leak if you serialize it into props, HTML, or an API response. Audit the entire data path, avoid logging secrets, and rotate exposed credentials. Build-time public configuration also matters when promoting one artifact between environments.

Question #077

078Next.js/Lead/Next.js 16.3; opt-inAdopt Instant Navigations without assuming they are default
The interview scenario

Next.js 16.3 includes an opt-in Instant Navigations model using cacheComponents and partialPrefetching. Structure routes with reusable cached content or streamed regions so useful UI can be available before the server response completes.

Prefetching is a cost and freshness decision, not a promise that every route is fully downloaded. Test realistic intent, network conditions, large link lists, and production behavior. Question #080
My notes & example from experience
081Web Platform/MidExplain the journey from URL to visible pixels
The interview scenario

A page has a fast API but still shows a blank screen for two seconds. Where would you investigate?

How to answer

Trace navigation, connection setup or reuse, the HTML response, parsing, critical CSS and scripts, layout, paint, and compositing. The browser can discover resources while parsing, but blocking resources or a client-only render dependency may postpone useful content. There is no universal fixed number of network round trips.

Use the network waterfall and performance trace to identify whether the bottleneck is server response, resource discovery, JavaScript work, styling, or rendering. Optimize the dependency that gates meaningful pixels rather than assuming a faster API fixes every blank screen.

Question #081
My notes & example from experience
082Web Platform/MidChoose defer, async, or module for a script
The interview scenario

An analytics script can run independently, but application scripts depend on the document and each other.

How to answer

For classic external scripts, defer downloads without blocking parsing and executes after parsing in document order, before DOMContentLoaded. Async executes when available and does not preserve document order, so it suits independent scripts. A regular classic script can block the parser.

Module scripts defer by default, load their dependency graph, and use module scope; adding async changes scheduling. Distinguish download timing from execution timing. Third-party scripts may still consume the main thread even when their loading does not block HTML parsing.

<script async src="/independent-analytics.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="/main.js"></script>

Common mistake

Using async on scripts that require a previous script to have executed.

Prove your answer

Throttle the network, randomize completion order, and inspect DOMContentLoaded plus long tasks.

Send an appropriately sized image and avoid hiding it behind client JavaScript or expensive rendering.

Use priority or preload selectively when a real discovery bottleneck exists. Good LCP is at most 2.5 seconds at the 75th percentile; field measurements and controlled lab traces answer different questions. Track the actual LCP element because it can vary across routes and viewports.

Question #083
My notes & example from experience
084Web Platform/SeniorImprove poor Interaction to Next Paint
The interview scenario

A filter button reacts slowly even though its click handler contains only a few lines.

How to answer

INP includes input delay, event processing, and presentation delay. Another long task can prevent the handler from starting, and expensive layout or rendering can postpone the next paint after it finishes. Inspect the entire interaction rather than only timing the callback.

Good INP is at most 200 milliseconds at the 75th percentile. Reduce main-thread contention, yield between noncritical chunks, move suitable pure computation to a worker, and keep immediate feedback cheap. A debounce can reduce work frequency but can also deliberately delay feedback.

Common mistake

Wrapping all work in a Promise and assuming it now runs off the main thread.

Prove your answer

Reproduce the slow interaction with CPU throttling and inspect its longest phase.

The interviewer goes deeperHow would you prioritize a spinner update versus expensive result computation?

Question #084
My notes & example from experience
085Web Platform/MidEliminate layout shifts during loading
The interview scenario

An article jumps when an ad, image, and web font finish loading.

How to answer

Reserve space for predictable asynchronous content using dimensions, aspect ratio, or stable placeholders. Avoid inserting unrequested content above what the user is reading. Font metric differences can also move text, so review fallback metrics and font loading strategy.

Good CLS is at most 0.1 at the 75th percentile. CLS uses session windows rather than a simple lifetime sum, and certain recent-input shifts are excluded. A single initial-load screenshot cannot reveal shifts caused by later ads or client navigation.

Question #085
My notes & example from experience
086Web Platform/SeniorDistinguish no-cache, no-store, and immutable
The interview scenario

Users see stale HTML after deployment, but content-hashed JavaScript files should be cached aggressively.

How to answer

no-cache permits storage but requires validation before reuse; it does not mean do not store. no-store tells caches not to store the response. For content-hashed public assets, a long max-age with immutable is suitable because changing bytes produces a new URL.

Use validators such as ETag for revalidation and separate browser policy from shared-cache policy. Personalized responses need explicit isolation and appropriate private or no-store behavior. Test the real CDN configuration; an application header can be modified by infrastructure.

Question #086
My notes & example from experience
087Web Platform/SeniorDebug CORS without weakening authentication
The interview scenario

An API works in curl, but a browser fetch from another origin fails. Someone suggests mode: no-cors.

How to answer

CORS controls whether browser JavaScript may read a cross-origin response; it is not authentication or a general server-to-server restriction. Certain requests first trigger an OPTIONS preflight. The server must allow the relevant origin, method, and headers.

Credentialed cross-origin requests need appropriate client credentials settings and explicit server permission; a wildcard origin is not valid for that credentialed access. no-cors usually gives JavaScript an opaque response, not readable API data. Inspect both preflight and actual request, plus cookie restrictions independently.

  credentials: "include"
}); // Requires correct server CORS and cookie policy.

Question #087
My notes & example from experience
088Web Platform/SeniorProtect cookie-authenticated mutations from CSRF
The interview scenario

A user is logged in with cookies. Could another website cause an unwanted transfer?

How to answer

Browsers can attach cookies automatically, so a malicious site may attempt a state-changing request using the victim's session. Use a deliberate CSRF defense: synchronizer tokens or an appropriate signed double-submit approach, trusted Origin checks, and framework protections where available.

SameSite is useful defense in depth, not a substitute for understanding deployment and cross-site flows. HttpOnly protects a cookie from direct script reads, not from being sent with requests; Secure limits transport to HTTPS. Authorization and input validation remain necessary. Never use GET for mutations.

Common mistake

Saying HttpOnly alone prevents CSRF, or assuming all subdomains are equally trusted.

Prove your answer

Attempt a cross-site form submission in a test environment and verify rejection without valid protection.

React text interpolation is safer than injecting HTML, but raw HTML sinks, unsafe URLs, custom Markdown renderers, and DOM APIs still require scrutiny. Treat CMS and model output as untrusted unless a carefully defined trust boundary proves otherwise.

Use a maintained sanitizer with an allowlist appropriate to the rendering context when HTML is genuinely necessary. Restrict dangerous URL schemes and avoid string-built event handlers. Keep sanitization aligned with later DOM transformations. Content Security Policy is defense in depth, not a replacement for safe output handling.

Question #089
My notes & example from experience
090Web Platform/Lead/React 19.3 integration; browser-dependentRoll out CSP and Trusted Types safely
The interview scenario

A security team requests CSP enforcement, but the application uses inline scripts and legacy HTML insertion.

How to answer

Inventory script sources and injection sinks, start with a reporting policy where appropriate, then narrow and enforce a nonce- or hash-based policy. Generate unpredictable per-response nonces when using nonces; never treat a fixed nonce as protection. Report-only observes violations without blocking them.

Trusted Types can constrain supported browser injection sinks to policy-produced values. A policy that simply trusts every string defeats its purpose. React 19.3 adds Trusted Types support, but application sanitization, browser support, third-party compatibility, and the actual CSP still require verification.

Common mistake

Adding unsafe-inline broadly to make every violation disappear, or blindly trusting strings in a policy.

Prove your answer

Test navigation, hydration, third-party widgets, and violation reporting in supported browsers.

Question #090
My notes & example from experience
091Web Platform/LeadHandle service-worker upgrades without stale applications
The interview scenario

A deployment succeeds, but some users keep running an old application shell and incompatible API client.

How to answer

A service worker has an installation, waiting, activation, and control lifecycle. A newly installed worker can wait while an old worker still controls open pages. Design update communication, cache naming, cleanup, and compatibility across tabs rather than forcing reloads indiscriminately.

skipWaiting and clients.claim can accelerate takeover, but may mix a new worker with an old loaded page. Consider a user-visible update prompt and protect unsaved work. Choose caching strategies by resource type; avoid indiscriminately caching authenticated responses or failed API results.

Common mistake

Assuming a hard reload always bypasses every cache or caching every GET response forever.

Prove your answer

Test two tabs, offline reloads, interrupted upgrades, and old client code against new responses.

Question #091

092Web Platform/SeniorRestore correctly from the back/forward cache
The interview scenario

Going Back restores a dashboard instantly, but a balance and login status are outdated.

How to answer

The back/forward cache may restore a frozen page including its DOM and JavaScript state, instead of performing a normal reload. Use pageshow and its persisted flag to recognize that restoration and revalidate sensitive or time-dependent information as required.

Avoid unnecessary unload handlers and audit eligibility with browser tools. Preserve the speed benefit instead of automatically forcing every restored page to reload. Authentication and authorization must still be checked on protected operations; a restored visual state is not proof of a valid session.

Question #092
My notes & example from experience
093Web Platform/SeniorChoose browser storage and synchronize tabs
The interview scenario

A large offline draft freezes typing when serialized into localStorage on every keystroke.

How to answer

Web Storage is synchronous, so repeated large serialization and writes can block the main thread. Keep tiny preferences there when appropriate; consider IndexedDB for larger structured data and asynchronous access. sessionStorage is scoped differently from localStorage and does not provide a shared cross-tab database.

Handle quota failures, privacy settings, and unavailable storage. The storage event can notify other same-origin documents about localStorage changes, but not the document that performed the write. Browser storage is accessible to origin scripts and is not a safe boundary against XSS.

Use a native button for actions and an anchor with href for navigation. A button supplies focus and keyboard behavior that a div does not automatically have. Provide an accessible name for icon-only controls and a visible focus indication.

Set type="button" when a button inside a form must not submit it. Use aria-pressed for a toggle when appropriate and communicate disabled state honestly. A custom control requires more than adding role="button"; native semantics are usually the simpler, more reliable foundation.

A modal needs an accessible name, sensible initial focus, contained tab navigation, Escape behavior where appropriate, and restoration of focus to the invoking control or a logical alternative. Background content must not remain interactable as though it were part of the modal flow.

Associate each field with a label and connect its error text using aria-describedby where appropriate. Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid after validation identifies a problem; do not rely on color alone. Preserve input so users can correct mistakes.

CSS width changes the display size, not necessarily the downloaded resource. Provide srcset candidates and an accurate sizes hint for width-based selection. Use picture when art direction or format alternatives are required, rather than assuming all responsive images are the same crop.

Question #097
My notes & example from experience
098Web Platform/SeniorLoad more results using an intersection observer
The interview scenario

An infinite list repeatedly fetches the same page when its loading sentinel stays on screen.

How to answer

IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports threshold crossings relative to a root. Use a sentinel and rootMargin to start loading before the user reaches the end, but guard with loading state, a stable cursor, and a hasMore condition. Visibility alone is not permission to create unlimited requests.

Disconnect or unobserve during cleanup and handle repeated callbacks. Preserve an accessible Load more control or equivalent navigation, meaningful loading feedback, and restoration behavior. Infinite scrolling affects focus, discoverability, browser history, and memory as well as fetching.

Prove your answer

Question #098
My notes & example from experience
099Web Platform/SeniorAvoid ResizeObserver feedback loops
The interview scenario

A responsive chart resizes its container inside a ResizeObserver callback and produces loop warnings.

How to answer

ResizeObserver reports element size changes, which is more targeted than listening only to window resize. Reading a size and then writing a value that changes the same observed size can create a feedback loop. Separate measurement from mutation and only apply genuinely changed target values.

Observe the correct box and handle device-pixel sizing when rendering a canvas. Scheduling a write for another frame can avoid same-cycle work, but does not repair a logical oscillation. Disconnect on teardown and avoid unnecessary React state updates for identical dimensions.

Common mistake

Assuming requestAnimationFrame alone makes a resize feedback loop correct.

Prove your answer

Resize the parent repeatedly, inspect warnings, and assert render counts stay bounded.
